newsitem.title: USA: Stocks appear fully valued -- NY Fed's McDonough.
newsitem.headline: Stocks appear fully valued -- NY Fed's McDonough.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of New York President William McDonough said Wednesday that U.S. stocks appeared fully valued but said he was not sure if they were overvalued.
Speaking at a breakfast meeting in New York City, McDonough said, "I have no idea," when asked if he thought the stock market was overvalued.
"Does it seem to be rather fully valued?," he asked. "By all conventional measures, yes."
The New York Fed President is vice chairman of the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee, which sets the nation's interest rates.

McDonough reiterated that he didn't know what the proper valuation of this or any other stock market is. "The real truth is, nobody else does either." He said the market sets a price and those prices are "usually reasonably rational."
McDonough said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's "irrational exuberance" remark, which he made in December, was not a statement, rather he was asking a question.
"I believe that was pulled out of context and the implication was that he made a statement," McDonough said. "He asked a question -- a very rational question," he said.

Greenspan's remark sent the Dow Jones industrial average reeling on concern that the central bank might raise interest rates to slow the upward drive in stocks, which have soared nearly 60 percent since 1995.
After a brief pause in December, stocks have been setting new highs in 1997, with the blue-chip Dow index closing Tuesday above 6,600 points for the first time.
McDonough did not appear to have had much of an impact on the stock market on Wednesday's trading, though the Dow was off 26.55 points at 6,574.11 in mid-afternoon.
